transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2027-05-05 15:00 UTC | Duration: 42 minutes | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Orbit VP Eng), Priya Patel (Orbit MLOps), Samir Rao (Orbit SRE)

Summary: quick weekly pilot sync to review latest throughput numbers, KV-cache warm/steady state behaviour, retune batching and concurrency, and agree next steps for a longer benchmark and security handoff. Customer wants to hit p95 latency goal while keeping cost per request under target; exploring a dedicated fallback test.

Topics: continuous batching, concurrency targets, queueing shape, KV cache hit-rate, tail latencies, hosted vs private fallback, telemetry/alerts.

Action items (recap): see action_items field.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. jordan, priy a, samir, good to see you. quick agenda — diego will run through the numbers, we want to get to a recommended concurrency / batch sweet spot and then align on next steps for the 6 hour run.
[00:18] Jordan Lee: yep sounds good. apologies, had a customer call earlier so i'm a little late, but i'm here.
[00:22] Diego Morales: cool, i'll share screen in a sec. um to start, high level: last week we saw average throughput of ~1.8k rps sustained across the pilot cluster with a 72% KV cache hit rate. p95 latency was around 210ms on hosted model variants, p50 at ~88ms.
[00:38] Priya Patel: 72% hit rate — is that steady or dip-y during bursts?
[00:42] Diego Morales: good question. it dipped to low 60s during the 30 minute burst test because cache warmup wasn't staged. when we pre-warmed keys for 20 minutes, it climbed to ~86% and p95 dropped to 160ms. so warm state matters a lot.
[01:02] Samir Rao: when you say pre-warm, what did you actually do — replay traffic or synthetic repeated keys?
[01:07] Diego Morales: replayed top-2000 keys using a weighted randomizer to mimic our prod skew. we also pinned cache TTL to 10 minutes for the run. i should note the KV cache labeling in the logs was sometimes recorded as K-V cache or kay-vee in the auto transcript, so if you see odd names that's why.
[01:23] Jordan Lee: makes sense. our production is more long-tail; we expect a bigger tail of user prompts. our histogram has a median token length of 56 but 10% are > 800 tokens. sharing that after this.
[01:36] Maya Chen: perfect, jordan. that helps pick batching and token budget defaults. diego, can you walk through the batching experiments?
[01:43] Diego Morales: sure. we tried continuous batching with two primary knobs: max batch size and target concurrency. initial config was max_batch=32, concurrency target=12. system averaged batch sizes around 18-22 because the queue fill latency prevented full 32 often. we then lowered max_batch to 16 while nudging concurrency to 18 and saw higher effective throughput with slightly lower p95.
[02:07] Priya Patel: wait — nudging concurrency up improved throughput even with smaller max_batch? i thought higher concurrency would increase overhead and maybe spike tail latency.
[02:15] Diego Morales: yes, typically. but in our runtime the batching combines many in-flight requests into micro-batches; by increasing concurrency we allowed the scheduler to form more parallel batches which smoothed queueing and reduced head-of-line blocking. the tradeoff is memory use and KV cache pressure — so we watch GPU memory and K-V cache eviction.
[02:36] Jordan Lee: do you have numbers for memory per concurrent worker? we have 2x A100-80G in the dedicated nodes.
[02:44] Diego Morales: for the quantized 4-bit model fork we tested, each extra concurrent stream added ~1.8GB of working set due to attention state and kv cache shards. so 18 concurrency on 80G is pushing it but still within margin depending on model length distribution.
[03:01] Samir Rao: that's useful. if concurrency leads to OOM risk at 18 we may prefer more nodes vs higher concurrency. cost tradeoff.
[03:09] Maya Chen: on cost — we modeled token costs and GPU-hours. the sweet spot for your 80/20 short/long prompt mix was around concurrency 14 with max_batch 20 for hosted fallback; that kept p95 near 150-170ms after warm state and put estimated infra cost ~12% under your internal threshold.
[03:28] Priya Patel: is the 150-170ms p95 after warm state including serialization and network?
[03:32] Diego Morales: yes, that's end-to-end measured from client SDK to first token out. intra-region network variance was small (<10ms) in our runs.
[03:41] Jordan Lee: you mentioned fallback — we'd like to test private/dedicated fallback in case hosted capacity drops. how do you handle model variants and automatic fallback?
[03:50] Maya Chen: our smart routing supports model variants and tiered capacity. policy can be set by latency priority or cost. for your case we recommend primary on hosted with a dedicated reserve that can be auto-activated when queue wait crosses threshold or we detect sustained p95 > 200ms. the handoff takes around 30-90s depending on how warmed the dedicated pool is.
[04:14] Samir Rao: 30 to 90 seconds — that's pretty wide. can we reduce warm time?
[04:18] Diego Morales: yes — keep a small warm pool or use burst capacity slices. pre-warmed KV cache is the bigger factor: if the dedicated pool has a persisted prefix cache or snapshot warm mechanism we can speed it to 10-20s for first tokens, but it's architecture dependent.
[04:34] Priya Patel: do you persist KV cache across workers? we have concerns about data residency and security.
[04:40] Maya Chen: KV cache contains request-derived keys, not raw PII. however, for privacy-conscious setups, in Private deployments you can disable shared cache or encrypt/cache per-tenant with KMS. we also have SOC2 artifacts and SSO options; priy a we'll start the security questionnaire as a next step.
[05:00] Jordan Lee: good. one operational question — queue shaping. during spikes we saw queue tails stretch and p99 blew past target. any immediate tuning for queue timeouts or admission control?
[05:10] Diego Morales: yes — two controls: hard concurrency cap per node and adaptive admission control that rejects or defers requests when queue depth exceeds shape thresholds. also backpressure headers to clients so you can retry with jitter. for this pilot we recommend setting queue depth cap to 300ms queue wait average and enabling soft-fallback to lower-capacity model variant at >350ms.
[05:34] Priya Patel: hmm our client library auto-retries, that could amplify spikes. we need to implement jitter + exponential backoff.
[05:41] Maya Chen: recommend changes: client-side max-retries=2, jitter window 200-600ms, and server-side 429 on overload with Retry-After. we'll include suggested client patch in the repo link.
[05:55] Jordan Lee: can you also explain the difference between continuous batching and naive batching? i want to make sure my team doesn't implement a naive batcher that waits too long.
[06:02] Diego Morales: continuous batching incrementally fills batches and emits when either max_size or max_wait is reached. naive batching might hold requests until a full batch which increases latency for low QPS. key knobs: max_batch_size, max_wait_ms (we use 20ms as default), and concurrency target. for your workload max_wait 12-20ms with adaptive concurrency gave best e2e tradeoffs.
[06:28] Samir Rao: about telemetry — what traces/logs do you recommend we collect?
[06:32] Diego Morales: per-request: queue_time_ms, batch_size, model_infer_ms, kv_cache_hit_bool, tokens_out, tokens_in. aggregate: p50/p95/p99 latency, batch size distribution, cache hit rate over time. also GPU mem pressure and evictions.
[06:49] Priya Patel: do you expose these via the console / Prometheus?
[06:52] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood Console exports Prom metrics and we can wire to your Datadog. we'll include a sample dashboard.
[06:59] Jordan Lee: okay numbers recap: last run 72% hit, p95 210 cold, 160 warm; recommended baseline concurrency 14, max_batch 20, max_wait 12-20ms. agreed?
[07:10] Diego Morales: agreed from our side. but i'd like to test an alternate: concurrency 22 + max_batch 12 for a different latency-throughput shape — it might reduce queue jitter for short prompts.
[07:22] Jordan Lee: let's run both.
[07:24] Maya Chen: yep — propose a 6-hour benchmark with the following schedule: first 2 hours baseline (concurrency 14, batch 20), next 2 hours alternate (concurrency 22, batch 12), final 2 hours stress bursts (10x bursts, simulate sudden traffic). diego will run and produce CSVs and histograms.
[07:43] Priya Patel: and include token-length stratification — short vs long distribution.
[07:47] Diego Morales: yes will include separate buckets and KV cache hit per bucket.
[07:51] Samir Rao: for the stress portion are you simulating retries? we want realistic amplification effects.
[07:56] Diego Morales: yes we'll integrate client retry behavior (max 2) and jitter. that will show whether retry amplification kills tail.
[08:03] Jordan Lee: switching gears — security and compliance. priy a wants SOC2 docs and a contact for the security team to start the SOC2 questionnaire.
[08:10] Maya Chen: i've got the SOC2 pack. priy a, i'll put you in touch with our security lead, daniel kwon, and he'll handle the questionnaire. also note we support SAML SSO, SCIM, and KMS integrations for private deployments.
[08:28] Priya Patel: great. also we need an audit log export for inference requests for compliance — is that available?
[08:33] Diego Morales: yes, we can stream audit logs to your S3 or to a SIEM. redaction rules can be applied before export.
[08:40] Jordan Lee: perfect. last topic: fallback correctness — if we route to a smaller model to maintain latency, how do you ensure outputs don't violate our quality gates?
[08:50] Diego Morales: we support quality gating by scores or canary thresholds. automated reranking or a simple reject-if-score-below threshold can be applied. for the pilot we can run parallel logging of fallback outputs and flag any regressions.
[09:05] Priya Patel: how about hallucination monitoring? we need evaluation sets.
[09:10] Maya Chen: Redwood Optimize can run evals on prompt sets and alert on regressions. we'll share an eval template and sample prompts you can use.
[09:18] Jordan Lee: ok let's talk timeline — when can you run the 6 hour and share results?
[09:22] Diego Morales: earliest tomorrow morning; i'll use the same cluster unless you want us to spin a separate one.
[09:27] Jordan Lee: separate cluster would be better to avoid impacting other tests; priy a ok?
[09:31] Priya Patel: yes separate cluster please.
[09:33] Maya Chen: noted. diego will provision a separate pilot cluster and run the schedule. results by 2027-05-07 EOD.
[09:41] Samir Rao: on instrumentation, can we get raw trace links? we want to correlate with our APM.
[09:46] Diego Morales: yes — we'll include per-request trace IDs and a mapping file.
[09:50] Jordan Lee: any quick wins before the benchmark?
[09:53] Diego Morales: pre-warm the KV cache for top keys and apply client-side retry jitter. both are low-effort and high-impact.
[09:59] Priya Patel: we'll start the client patch today.
[10:02] Maya Chen: sweet. anything else?
[10:05] Jordan Lee: one more — can you share the batch tuning spreadsheet now so we can model cost vs latency for our CFO?
[10:10] Maya Chen: yes i'll send it after this call.
[10:12] Priya Patel: and please include the dedicated fallback estimate for 2x A100 nodes.
[10:16] Diego Morales: will do.
[10:18] Maya Chen: ok recap of next steps — run 6hr (diego), send benchmark template + cost spreadsheet (maya), security intro (maya) and kv warm experiment (diego). Jordan will provide traffic histogram. deliverables due early next week.
[10:31] Jordan Lee: good, thanks.
[10:33] Samir Rao: thanks all.
[10:34] Maya Chen: thanks — we'll follow up in email with links: deck: https://redwood.ai/pilot/deck-orbit, benchmark template: https://redwood.ai/pilot/bench-template, dashboard sample: https://redwood.ai/pilot/dash-sample.
[10:48] Priya Patel: noted. bye.
[10:50] END
